title: Let's grab a coffee!
goal: Make a phone call, invite a friend out, accept and turn down invitations — while using dative pronouns as **recipients**: who you give, say, write, and send things to.
bekal: use *îmi, îți, îi, ne, vă, le* as recipients, including doubling: *Îi scriu Ioanei*
choose the right form after a preposition: *cu mine, pentru tine, la noi*
invite with *hai să…* and *ce-ar fi să…*, then say no without giving offense

dialogs.title: Dialogue — La telefon
dialogs.intro: Thursday evening. Andrei has concert tickets for Saturday, and Budi wants to invite Ioana. He calls, but the one who answers is Maria, Ioana's younger sister.

notes: **Îți trimit un mesaj.** This is the heart of the unit. You know the dative pronouns *îmi, îți, îi…* from *îmi place* (unit 10), but there they felt like part of a set phrase. Here their job is clear: they mark the **recipient**. *Îți trimit* = "I'll send (to) you", *îi spun* = "I'll tell him/her". English often needs "to"; Romanian manages with one syllable before the verb.

**Îi spun și lui Andrei.** When the recipient is named, the short pronoun **stays** — the same doubling as *Îl cunosc pe Andrei* in unit 12. A man's name gets *lui* in front; a woman's name ending in *-a* changes to *-ei*: *Îi scriu Ioanei.* That's the genitive-dative form from unit 13, now doing its second job.

**E pentru tine! Bilete pentru noi.** After a preposition, pronouns take the stressed form. Only two are really new: *eu → mine* and *tu → tine* — like English *I → me*. The rest are the same as the subject forms. So *cu mine*, not *cu eu*.

**Hai să mergem!** *Hai* is an all-purpose "come on, let's". It's followed by *să* + the *noi* subjunctive (unit 11): *hai să mergem, hai să bem, hai să vedem*. It can even go with no verb at all: *Hai la o cafea!* A more careful option: *Ce-ar fi să…?* — "how about…?". *Ar fi* is the conditional of *a fi*, which comes at the next level; for now learn it whole.

**Îmi pare rău, nu pot. Am de lucru.** The most natural way to decline: apologize, say no, give a short reason. *Îmi pare rău* is literally "it seems bad to me" — the dative again. *Am de lucru* = "I have (something) to work on"; the pattern *am de* + verb/noun is handy: *am de învățat* (I have to study), *am de scris un e-mail*.

grammars.title: The dative as recipient: to whom?
body: Verbs of giving, saying, writing, sending, and showing have two objects: **what** is given (accusative) and **to whom** (dative). The recipient appears as a short, unstressed pronoun before the verb.

head: Who
Dative
Example
Meaning
rows: Will you give me your number?

after: **Doubling is required** when the recipient is named: *Îi dau **lui Andrei** cartea.* *Îi scriu **Ioanei**.* *Le spun **părinților**.* *Îi trimit **doamnei Popescu** chiria.* The short pronoun can't be dropped, even if it sounds redundant to English ears.

**Verbs that take the dative:** *a da* (give), *a spune* (say, tell), *a scrie* (write), *a trimite* (send), *a arăta* (show), *a explica* (explain), *a răspunde* (answer), *a mulțumi* (thank), *a telefona* (phone), *a cere* (ask for).

**Watch out for *a suna*:** this most common verb for "to call" takes the **accusative**: *Te sun mai târziu. O sun pe Ioana. Vă sun mâine.* *A telefona*, on the other hand, takes the dative: *Îi telefonez Ioanei.* Same meaning; different grammar.

**Short hyphenated forms** turn up in three places you know: after *nu* (*nu-mi spune, nu-ți dau, nu-i scriu*), after *să* (*Poți să-mi dai…? Vreau să-i spun…*), and in the past tense (*mi-a dat, ți-am spus, i-am scris, le-am trimis* — unit 15). In the imperative they move to the end: *Spune-mi! Dă-mi! Scrie-i!*
**A little trap:** *îi* and *le* have two jobs each. *Îi văd* = "I see them" (accusative m pl), but *îi spun* = "I tell him/her" (dative singular). The verb decides.

grammars.title: After prepositions: mine, tine, el, ea…
body: Short pronouns never stand after a preposition. In that position the stressed form is used — and the good news is that only two differ from the subject forms.

head: Subject
After a preposition
Example
Meaning
rows: I have a message from them.

after: ***La mine, la tine, la noi*** means "at/to my place, your place, our place": *Hai la mine!* (come over to my place), *Diseară mâncăm la noi.* Very common in invitations.

***Pe mine, pe tine*** are used to stress the object, and the short pronoun stays too: *Pe mine mă cheamă Budi. Pe tine te-am văzut ieri.* Likewise the dative has emphatic forms from unit 10: *Mie îmi dai cafeaua, lui îi dai ceaiul.*
These forms are also used after *decât* and *ca* in comparisons (unit 18): *Ioana vorbește mai repede decât mine.*

**Three levels of invitation:** *Hai la film!* (spontaneous, casual) → *Hai să mergem la film!* (a clear invitation) → *Ce-ar fi să mergem la film?* (a polite suggestion). To several people, or someone you address formally, *hai* becomes *haideți*: *Haideți să mergem!*

head: Sentence
English

May I speak to Mrs. Popescu?
*Vă sun mai târziu.* · *Te sun mai târziu.*
I'll call you back later. (polite · informal)
*Nu te aud bine. Nu am semnal.*
I can't hear you well. I have no signal.

blocks.text: On the phone Romanians introduce themselves with *sunt* + name ("I am…"), not with "this is". The technical vocabulary is almost all familiar: *telefon, mesaj, număr, semnal, baterie, e-mail, aplicație*. Three verbs to practice: *a suna* (to call; *sun, suni, sună* — also "to ring": *Sună telefonul!*), *a trimite* (to send; *trimit, trimiți, trimite*), and *a răspunde* (to answer; *răspund, răspunzi, răspunde*): *Nu răspunde* — "he/she isn't picking up".

blocks.title: Phone manners
items: A casual call rarely ends with a single *pa*. The usual thing is a string: *Bine, hai, pa, pa!* — and *hai* here isn't an invitation but a "well, OK then".
With family and close friends people sign off with ***Te pup!*** — literally "I kiss you", like "hugs and kisses" at the end of a message. Don't be surprised, and don't use it with your boss.
With older women, *Sărut mâna* from unit 17 still works on the phone, at the start or the end.
Romanian cell numbers start with **07**, and the country code is **+40**. Numbers are read out in groups of two or three digits — good practice for the numbers in unit 5.

head: Sentence
English
Used for
rows: *Ești liber diseară?* (to a man) · *Ești liberă diseară?* (to a woman)
Do you want to come with us?
How about going to the mountains?
Where shall we meet? What time?
*Ne vedem la șapte, în fața cinematografului.*
Let's meet at seven, in front of the movie theater.

blocks.text: Note *liber / liberă*: the adjective agrees with the person **being asked**, so Budi asks Ioana *Ești liberă?*, and Ioana asks Budi *Ești liber?* *Diseară* = tonight; *mâine-seară* = tomorrow evening. Declining with no reason sounds cold, and a long reason sounds made up — one short sentence plus *poate altă dată* is just right. If you really do want to meet, suggest another day on the spot, like Budi: *Atunci ce-ar fi să… duminică?*

blocks.title: "Hai la o cafea" is rarely just about coffee
items: *Hai la o cafea!* means "let's hang out and talk". The coffee may turn into lemonade or beer, and one cup can last three hours — especially on the terraces of the Old Town in summer.

***Fac eu cinste!*** = "my treat!". Whoever does the inviting often offers to pay; next time it's your turn. To split the bill, the phrase is ***plătim nemțește*** — literally "we pay the German way".
Being fifteen minutes late for a casual meetup is still forgiven; Romanians call it the *sfertul academic*, "the academic quarter hour". For work and doctor's appointments, be on time.
